1 · Europe: is it getting more extreme?
We count the country-months above 1: one country with one extreme month = 1. With all 45 countries, a year has 540 country-months for each component.

1.1 Each hazard has its own story
One small chart per component (small multiples): every bar is the share of country-months above 1 in one year, the dashed line is the average of 1981–2010.
💬 Compare each bar with the dashed line: which hazards have become more frequent since 1981–2010, which rarer, which show no clear trend?
Now the same hazards from another angle: when in the year do they strike?


1.2 When in the year?
A rose for each hazard and period, inspired by Florence Nightingale’s diagrams (1858). How to read it: * every petal is a calendar month: January at the top, then clockwise (April on the right, July at the bottom, October on the left); * the area of a petal, not its length, is proportional to the share of country-months that were extreme in that month, as in Nightingale’s roses; * inside each petal the classes go from the centre outwards: 1–2 (the lightest shade), 2–3, above 3 (the darkest); * top row: the first period, bottom row: the second one (chosen in PERIODS).
Remember: every month is compared with the same month of 1981–2010, so an extreme in winter is unusual for winter.
💬 Compare the two rows: a rose that grows in every direction means more extremes all year round; a petal that grows alone points to one season.

3 · One country, zoom in
After Europe as a whole, we zoom in on one country, chosen in COUNTRY in the next cell: the charts below show it from several angles, down to its regions.
Countries you can choose (from the menu in the next cell): Albania, Andorra, Austria, Belarus, Belgium, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Faroes, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Guernsey, Hungary, Iceland, Ireland, Isle of Man, Italy, Jersey, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Moldova, Montenegro, Netherlands, North Macedonia, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Serbia, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Turkey, Ukraine, United Kingdom.

3.1 The barcode of extremes
Inspired by Ed Hawkins’ warming stripes: one row per component, one cell per year.


3.2 Month by month, as in the Data Station
One component only. Every bar is one month, coloured by E3CI class; the dots mark the TOP_N most intense months on record, with their value.
💬 Where are the darkest bars, above 3: spread over the whole period, or concentrated in the last years?


3.3 Records: are they falling faster than chance would predict?
The same months, seen through their records. A record is a month with a higher E3CI than every month before it in the same country, since January 1981. In a climate that does not change, records become rarer and rarer: after 10 years the chance that a month beats all the previous ones is about 1 in 120; after 40 years, about 1 in 480. That’s why records are counted only from START_YEAR (1991 by default): in the first years almost every month is a record, because there is hardly any history to beat.
📐 How many records should we expect? In a stable climate each of the first n months has the same chance of being the highest, so month n sets a record with probability 1/n. Adding up 1/n over the months since START_YEAR gives the number of records we would expect if nothing were changing. It is a reference, not an exact forecast: anomalies persist from one month to the next, so records can come in clusters.
💬 Compare the records observed with those expected in a stable climate (in the title): many more records than chance, especially in the last years, are a sign of a changing climate.


3.4 Which months, which years?
The same data as a heatmap: rows are months, columns are years. Top: extreme months per year. Right: how often each calendar month was extreme, then (grey) and now (colour).


3.5 A real event
Many events hit only one region: here we use the regional data. Choose an event in CASE: was it the most intense month on record in its region? How does it compare with the rest of Europe?


3.6 One month, region by region
Like chart 2.1, one level down: one component in one month, every year, in the regions of the country chosen at the top of Part 3.

text:
1 · Europe: is it getting more extreme? ⏱ 8 min
We count the country-months above 1: one country in extreme heat for one month = 1. With 45 countries and 12 months, a year has 540 country-months for each component.

1.1 Each hazard has its own story
One small chart per component (small multiples): every bar is the share of country-months above 1 in one year, the dashed line is the average of 1981–2010.









💬 Since 2011, months of extreme heat have been more than 3 times as frequent as in 1981–2010, and fire-weather extremes almost 3 times, while cold extremes and hail have become rarer. Precipitation, wind and drought change less, and less regularly: trends in these hazards are harder to detect than in temperature.
Now let’s look at the same hazards from another angle: when in the year do they strike?


1.2 When in the year?
A rose for each hazard and period, inspired by Florence Nightingale’s diagrams (1858). How to read it: * every petal is a calendar month: January at the top, then clockwise (April on the right, July at the bottom, October on the left); * the area of a petal, not its length, is proportional to the share of country-months that were extreme in that month, as in Nightingale’s roses; * inside each petal the classes go from the centre outwards: 1–2 (the lightest shade), 2–3, above 3 (the darkest); * top row: 1981–2010; bottom row: since 2011.
Remember: an E3CI “heat extreme” in January is an unusually warm January, not a 40 °C day.









💬 In 1981–2010 most roses are almost round: the E3CI measures every month against the same month of that period. Since 2011 the extreme-heat rose has grown in every direction: in every calendar month, from a quarter to almost half of the country-months were extreme, against about one in ten before. Fire weather grows above all in spring and summer (in April, from 5% to 20% of the country-months), while the cold rose shrinks, especially in summer and in late autumn.

Inspired by Ed Hawkins’ warming stripes: one row per component, one cell per year.




















3.2 Month by month, as in the Data Station
Now one component only: extreme heat. Every bar is one month, coloured by E3CI class; the dots mark the three most intense months on record, with their value.









💬 The darkest bars, above 3, are almost all recent: 4 months in the 30 years 1981–2010, 31 since 2011. And the three most intense months on record are October 2023, April 2024 and July 2026 (remember: an extreme October is an unusually warm October, not a 40 °C day).


3.3 Records: are they falling faster than chance would predict?

💬 Since 1991 Italy has set 6 records of extreme heat, where a stable climate would give about 1.5, and 3 of them in the last ten years alone (April 2018, October 2022, October 2023), when about 0.2 would be expected. Every step of the staircase raises the bar, and yet the bar keeps being beaten.


3.4 Which months, which years?
The same data as a heatmap: rows are months, columns are years. Top: extreme months per year. Right: how often each calendar month was extreme, then (grey) and now (colour).

The first cell lists other famous events: in the second part of the workshop you can choose one of them.











3.6 Rain in October, region by region
One month, every year, in the regions of the country chosen at the top of Part 3 (here the 20 Italian regions): rain in October. Why October?
